Q: How can I prevent duplicate JSON-LD schema output in WordPress? A:

The safest approach is to avoid generating a second LocalBusiness entity when Rank Math is already describing the same business.

Multiple JSON-LD blocks are not inherently a problem. The problem is having two separate entities that represent the same business but contain conflicting or redundant information.

With Rank Math, I would first inspect the final HTML source and determine what it is already generating. If it has a LocalBusiness/Organization entity, modify that schema through Rank Math's schema filters rather than outputting another <script> block from wp_head.

For example, Rank Math exposes filters that can be used to modify its schema graph:

add_filter( 'rank_math/json_ld', function( $data, $jsonld ) {

    // Modify the existing schema graph here.

    return $data;

}, 10, 2 );

The exact structure of $data depends on the schema Rank Math has generated, so I would inspect the array before modifying it rather than assuming a particular node/key exists.

If the information you need is not appropriate for Rank Math's existing entity, adding a separate JSON-LD block can be perfectly valid. In that case, give the entities stable @id values and reference the same business where appropriate instead of creating two unrelated descriptions.

For example:

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "LocalBusiness",
  "@id": "https://example.com/#business",
  "name": "Example Business",
  "url": "https://example.com/"
}

Then other schema nodes can reference that entity using:

{
  "@id": "https://example.com/#business"
}

So I would use this order of preference:

  1. Check the rendered HTML and identify every schema source.

  2. If Rank Math already creates the business entity, extend/modify that entity.

  3. If Rank Math cannot represent the required data, add a separate schema node and connect it with @id where appropriate.

  4. Remove redundant schema generated by another plugin/theme/custom code if it describes the same entity unnecessarily.

  5. Test the final rendered page, rather than only the PHP code, after clearing any page/cache/CDN layers.

Also, don't treat Google's Rich Results Test reporting multiple entities as proof that the JSON-LD is invalid. A page can legitimately contain multiple schema entities. What matters is whether those entities represent distinct things or whether several independent nodes are redundantly describing the same business.

In this case, I would not disable Rank Math's schema blindly. I'd inspect its generated graph first and modify or extend it where possible.

Q: Can Xpath expressions access shadow-root elements? A:

If you are using Selenium, you can get the parent element that contains the shadow root by its xpath. Then you need to retrieve the shadow root, e.g. in Python

shadow_root = driver.find_element(By.XPATH, '//div[@id="something"]').shadow_root

Using the retrieved shadow root you can now use xpath inside it to retrieve elements.

Q: Active Directory: Password history check before lock out user A:

These are the results testing with MS Server 2022 I did as part of a theses. I used "Active Directory - Users and Computer" to change the password of the user of concern. For Kerberos and NTLM Auth, I used "LDP.exe", for RADIUS I used "eapol_test" and for LDAP testing "Apache Directory Studio".

L Auth N N-1 N-2 N-3
0 Kerberos S B B B
NTLM/RADIUS/LDAP* S B B B
1 Kerberos S F B B
NTLM/RADIUS/LDAP* S F B B
2 Kerberos S F F B
NTLM/RADIUS/LDAP* S TU BU B
3 Kerberos S F F B
NTLM/RADIUS/LDAP* S TU FU B
4 Kerberos S F F B
NTLM/RADIUS/LDAP* S TU FU B
  • L: Number of last used passwords of a user to be stored (pwdHistoryLength / Enforce password history with ... entries)
  • Auth: Authentication method
  • N: Currently valid password
  • N-1: Previously chosen password
  • *: Other tested authentication methods: NTLM (protocol), RADIUS (MSCHAPv2 / PEAP-MS-CHAPv2) via Network Policy Server, LDAP Simple Bind
  • S: Success
  • B: Failed, badPwdCount is increased
  • F: Failed, badPwdCount is not increased
  • T: Success within a period of 5 minutes after password change, thereafter failure, badPwdCount is not increased
  • U: Undocumented or partially undocumented behavior

For instance, if Enforce password history with ... entries (L) is set to 3, and the user supplies the previously valid password (N-1, might be stored as WiFi or IMAP password or similar), the result is T: Their authentication was successful for ~5 min after the password was changed, and afterwards, log in failed but badPwdCount was not incremented.

TLDR: Set Enforce password history (AD attribute: pwdHistoryLength, PowerShell Property PasswordHistoryCount) to a value between 3 and 24, applying the policy gpupdate /force, and change the password at least twice afterwards, then, the issue will vanquish. I am by no means a Windows Expert/Insider. The entire behavior differs slightly from Microsoft's description for Server 2003, and the fact that no source code is available for auditing, is troublesome - for a component that is the heart of many institutions.

Enforce password history can be set in Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Account Policies → Password Policy → Enforce password history

Q: can C# JIT elimination of virtual function calls here? A:

The jitter should specialize the compare method for each T, and that should allow for inlining. But it is always difficult to tell what the jitter will do without inspecting the produced assembly. So rather than making guesses we should measure. I.e. compare your generic variant with a non-generic variant that is already inlined.

When I do this I get about 7.5s for the non-generic vs 9.8s for the generic (with.net 10), so a small difference. I do not know exactly why, but more abstract code is often more difficult to optimize for the jitter. But this difference is completely irrelevant since the built in Array.Sort takes 40ms for the same data.

Before any optimizations you should start any optimization by first establishing that there is a performance problem. I.e. if you know you will run your sort algorithm 10 times when learning to program, performance does not really matter.

This illustrates why algorithm selection should be the first step if you do need to optimize. Improving the algorithm can result in many order of magnitudes of improvements. Much larger than most micro optimizations.

If you do attempt any micro optimizations you should measure carefully to ensure you are actually making improvements. And be aware that goals like abstraction and readability is often in opposition to performance. Highly optimized code is often close to unreadable unless there are more comments explaining the code than there is code.
